# Prediction ITU R 1812 model 

This script uses the ITU R 1812 model to make predictions on whether a location is covered by LoRa from a certain gateway location. The model is written in python code (https://github.com/eeveetza/Py1812), hence this script makes the input for the python script and reads the output of the python script using R.
The model uses several sources of input:
- Height:
  - DTM: Digital terrain model to estimate landscape heights along connectivity distances
  - Heights of vegetation: Estimate per BWK polygon (calculated in preparatory_steps_ITUR_predictions.Rmd)
  - Gateway heights
  - Sensor node heights
- Hardware specifications:
  - Sensor: 
    - Antenna Gain
    - Transmission power
  - Gateway:
    - Antenna Gain
    - Cable loss
    - Sensitivity per Spreading Factor 
- Other model specifications:
  - Frequency (always 868 MHz for European LoRa)
  - Percentage of time transmission loss not exceeded
  - Percentage of location transmission loss not exceeded
  - Distance_interval: Interval in which to take "steps" along the connection distance (smaller = better but more computational intensive)

All input for the python script is should be put in "ITU_R_Predictions/Py1812-main/data".
The correct preparations to run this script are done in "ITU_R_Predictions/Rscripts/Preparatory_steps_ITUR_predictions.Rmd" --> Be sure to run this script before this one (with the same parameters!)
The eventual output can be found in "ITU_R_Predictions/Intermediate/".


```{r data & libraries, include=FALSE}

library(ggplot2) # Plotting
library(mapview) # Spatial exploration
library(dplyr) # Data wrangling
library(sf) # Spatial handling
library(fistools) # Google drive function
library(jsonlite) # JSON file writer
library(reticulate) # Python connection
library(patchwork) # For putting plots side-by-side

source("ITU_R_Predictions/Functions/get_dhmv_wcs.R")

# This is now your stable, local path
env_path <- file.path(getwd(), "ITU_R_Predictions/python_env")

# Create the environment from scratch
if (!virtualenv_exists(env_path)) {
  virtualenv_create(env_path)
  virtualenv_install(env_path, packages = c(
    "numpy", 
    "pandas", 
    "geopandas", 
    "rasterio", 
    "tqdm", 
    "shapely", 
    "pyproj"
  ))
}

# Point R to the new local engine
use_virtualenv(env_path, required = TRUE)


### Simple things to change as inputs
## Check that the distance and study area are the same as prepared in "Preparatory_steps_ITUR_predictions.Rmd"

# Study area
sa <- read.csv("ITU_R_Predictions/Input/study_area.csv") %>%
  filter(name == "MERELBEKE") # Choose which gateway location to simulate for

# Distance for the simulation (in meter and currently minimally 2000)
sim_dist <- 5000

# Gateway antenna gain (hardware specification)
gw_antenna_db <- 5

# Gateway height (in meter)
gw_height <- 7

```

We need the Digital Terrain Model of our study area, but since this is too large for local saving or on Github, we work with WCS service to just download the necessary tiles

```{r get spatial data}

sa_sf <- st_as_sf(
  sa,
  coords = c("lon","lat"),
  crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 31370) %>%
  # Radius of 5 km
  st_buffer(dist = sim_dist)

# Download the digital terrain model in case it is missing (too large for Github)
dtm <- get_dhmv_wcs_tiled(
  "DHMVII_DTM_1m", 
  st_bbox(sa_sf),
  resolution = 1,
  tile_size = 2000)
  
terra::writeRaster(dtm, 
                   "ITU_R_Predictions/Py1812-main/data/dtm_height_model.tif",
                   filetype = "GTiff",
                   overwrite = T)

```

# Specify all parameters for the ITU R model

```{r ITU R specifications}

# Sensor specifications
sensor_height = 1 
antenna_gain_sensor = 2.0 
transmission_power = 6.0

# Gateway hardware specifications
antenna_gain_gateway = gw_antenna_db
cable_loss_gateway = 2.0

# Spreading factor limits
sf7_sens = -123 
sf8_sens = -126
sf9_sens = -129
sf10_sens = -132
sf11_sens = -134.5
sf12_sens = -137

# General specifications
grid_cell_size = 30
grid_square = F
lora_frequency = 0.868
percentage_time = 50
percentage_locations = 95
interval_evaluation = 20

# Specific characteristics
output_name = sa[1,1] # Change this if multiple are in one file
specific_gateways = T

```

# Create hexagonal grid over national park
We use hexagonal grids to limit corner effects
The LoRa connectivity will be estimated for each single grid cell, hence decreasing cell size increases computation time.

```{r grid creation}

# Make a grid of xxx by xxx meters (hexagonal to limit corner effects)
grid <- st_make_grid(sa_sf, cellsize = c(grid_cell_size, grid_cell_size), square = grid_square)

# Visualization
ggplot() +
 geom_sf(data = grid) +
 geom_sf(data = sa_sf, col = "blue", fill = NA)

# Transform the grid into an sf object
grid_sf <- st_sf(geometry = grid)

# Give each cell of the grid an identicator
grid_sf$id <- 1:nrow(grid_sf)

# Save grid to python data source
st_write(grid_sf, "ITU_R_Predictions/Py1812-main/data/study_area_hex_grid.shp", append = F)

```

# Specify all necessary input for ITU R model
Here we specify all the necessary input that the python script needs to fuel the ITU R model. The gateways_list is only necessary when we want to specify specific gateways.
All others are dependent on the hardware of sensors and gateways, and specific conditions.

```{r gateway locations}

x <- st_centroid(sa_sf)[[2]][[1]][1]
y <- st_centroid(sa_sf)[[2]][[1]][2]

# 1. Define a list of Gateways
gateways_list <- list(
 list(id = output_name, x = x, y = y, height = gw_height))

# 2. Add them to the global settings
simulation_params <- list(
 # Gateway locations and heights
 gateways = gateways_list,
 
 # Sensor specifications
 sensor = list(
   height = sensor_height, 
   antenna_gain = antenna_gain_sensor, 
   tx_power = transmission_power),

 # Hardware specifications of gateway
 hardware = list(
   antenna_gain_gw = antenna_gain_gateway, 
   cable_loss_gw = cable_loss_gateway, 
   sensitivity_sf7 = sf7_sens, 
   sensitivity_sf8 = sf8_sens, 
   sensitivity_sf9 = sf9_sens, 
   sensitivity_sf10 = sf10_sens, 
   sensitivity_sf11 = sf11_sens, 
   sensitivity_sf12 = sf12_sens), # Based on The Things Network

 # Other model specifications
 model = list(
   max_dist = sim_dist,
   freq_GHz = lora_frequency, 
   time_percentage = percentage_time, 
   loc_percentage = percentage_locations, 
   distance_interval = interval_evaluation),
 
 grid_size = list(grid_cell_size = grid_cell_size),
 
 # Output specifications
 output = list(output_name = output_name)
)

# 3. Write the JSON
write_json(simulation_params, "ITU_R_Predictions/Py1812-main/data/sim_settings.json", auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE)

```

# Python script
Now lets run the python script using all of the data prepared here.
(Be careful however, this script will have to evaluate +- 800 000 cells, taking up to three days)

```{r python ITU-R model, include=FALSE}

# Keep environment from before python
pre_python_env <- ls()

# Using here::here() is the gold standard for GitHub portability
base_path <- here::here("ITU_R_Predictions/Py1812-main")

# 1. Prepare Python environment
py_run_string(paste0("import sys; sys.path.append('", base_path, "/src')"))

# 2. Run the simulation
# We use source_python, but reticulate now handles the environment automatically
source_python(file.path(base_path, "heatmap_builder_R.py"))

# 3. Clean up R's memory (optional)
rm(list=setdiff(ls(), pre_python_env))

unlink("ITU_R_Predictions/Py1812-main/data/dtm_height_model.tif")

```

# First look at results

Since even the .zip folder of this specific case is too large for Github, we moved it (manually) to the google drive. Hence, we will first have to download the .zip folder, unzip it and read both gateway locations and predictions.

```{r read results}

# Download .zip folder
# fistools::download_gdrive_if_missing(
#   "1ZH0_dWQVEdfG2TXNihCLyqFUkw8JV8-D",
#   paste0("ITU_R_Predictions/Intermediate/", output_name, ".zip"))

# First unzip the results
unzip(paste0("ITU_R_Predictions/Intermediate/", output_name, ".zip"),
      exdir = paste0("ITU_R_Predictions/Intermediate/", output_name))

# Gateways
gateways <- st_read(paste0("ITU_R_Predictions/Intermediate/", output_name, "/", output_name, "_gws.shp"))

# Predictions
pred_csv <- read.csv(paste0("ITU_R_Predictions/Intermediate/", output_name, "/", output_name, ".csv")) %>%
  filter(sf12_ok != 0)

meta <- jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0("ITU_R_Predictions/Intermediate/", output_name, "/metadata.json"))

# Grid
grid_sf <- read_sf("ITU_R_Predictions/Py1812-main/data/study_area_hex_grid.shp")

# nphk intersection to remove all the rest
grid_sf <- st_intersection(grid_sf, sa_sf)

# cleanup
unlink(paste0("ITU_R_Predictions/Intermediate/", output_name), recursive = T)

```

# Processing of data
Instead of plotting the six different spreading factor layers on top eachother, we will first create a new single layer where each unique cell is one row provided with a the best SF reaching this cell and the amount of gateways

```{r results processing}

# Just as an indication: How much of the NPHK is covered?
n_distinct(pred_csv[pred_csv$cell_id %in% grid_sf$id,]$cell_id) / n_distinct(grid_sf$id) *100

# First aggregate the data to reduce difficulty of calculation
# This turns 400k rows into ~80k rows (one per unique cell)
cell_summary <- pred_csv %>%
  group_by(cell_id) %>%
  summarize(
    # Count how many rows (gateways) had succesfull sf12 connection
    gw_count = sum(sf12_ok == 1),
    
    # Logic to find the best SF across ALL gateways for this cell
    # we use max() on the _ok columns to see if ANY gateway reached it
    sf7_any  = max(sf7_ok),
    sf8_any  = max(sf8_ok),
    sf9_any  = max(sf9_ok),
    sf10_any = max(sf10_ok),
    sf11_any = max(sf11_ok),
    sf12_any = max(sf12_ok),
    
  ) %>%
  # Filter out cells with zero coverage
  filter(gw_count > 0) %>%
  # Determine the best SF label
  mutate(best_sf = case_when(
    sf7_any  == 1 ~ "SF7",
    sf8_any  == 1 ~ "SF8",
    sf9_any  == 1 ~ "SF9",
    sf10_any == 1 ~ "SF10",
    sf11_any == 1 ~ "SF11",
    sf12_any == 1 ~ "SF12"
  )) %>%
  mutate(best_sf = factor(best_sf, levels = c("SF7", "SF8", "SF9", "SF10", "SF11", "SF12")),
         gw_count = factor(gw_count, levels = c("5", "4", "3", "2", "1")))  %>%
  inner_join(x = grid_sf, by = c("id" = "cell_id"))


# --- 2. PLOT A: BEST SF ---
p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = sa_sf, fill = "white", color = "grey80") +
  geom_sf(data = cell_summary, aes(fill = best_sf, color = best_sf)) +
  geom_sf_label(data = gateways, aes(label = id), size = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colorRampPalette(c("blue3", "darkorange"))(6), name = "Best SF") +
  scale_color_manual(values = colorRampPalette(c("blue3", "darkorange"))(6), name = "Best SF") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Best Available Spreading Factor") +
  plot_annotation(title = paste("Simulation:", meta$run_info$name),
                  subtitle = paste("Run at:", meta$run_info$date, "; with gateway height of ", meta$parameters$gateways$height, " m & antenna gain of ", meta$parameters$hardware$antenna_gain_gw, " dB"),
                  theme = theme(
                    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, vjust = 0.30, size = 20),
                    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, vjust = 0.25))
                  )

# Save the plot to a correct location based on its output name
ggsave(paste0("ITU_R_Predictions/Output/", output_name, ".png"),
       plot = p1,
       width = 12, height = 8, dpi = 600)


```

# Other visualizations

```{r Other visualizations}
library(ggmap)

# Register your Google API key once
register_google(key = "AIzaSyACdSg_xkX_gdKzSQiZQETStjEDOC_HVZg")

# 1. Reproject data to WGS 84
sa_sf_wgs       <- st_transform(sa_sf, 4326)
cell_summary_wgs <- st_transform(cell_summary, 4326)
gateways_wgs     <- st_transform(gateways, 4326)

# 2. Get the bounding box of your region
bbox <- st_bbox(sa_sf_wgs)
names(bbox) <- c("left", "bottom", "right", "top")

# 3. Fetch Google Map tile ("roadmap", "satellite", "terrain", or "hybrid")
gmap <- get_googlemap(
  center = c(lon = mean(bbox[c("left", "right")]), lat = mean(bbox[c("bottom", "top")])),
  zoom = 13,
  maptype = "hybrid"
)

# 4. Plot using ggmap() as the base
p2 <- ggmap(gmap) +
  geom_sf(data = cell_summary_wgs, aes(fill = best_sf), alpha = 0.6, color = NA, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_sf_label(data = gateways_wgs, aes(label = id), size = 2, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colorRampPalette(c("blue3", "darkorange"))(6), name = "Best SF") +
  # scale_color_manual(values = colorRampPalette(c("blue3", "darkorange"))(6), name = "Best SF") +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(4326)) + # Ensure correct spatial alignment
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Best Available Spreading Factor")

p2

# Using mapview

# Define the same color palette (6 colors)
sf_colors <- colorRampPalette(c("blue3", "darkorange"))(6)

# Build and combine layers
map_out <- mapview(
    sa_sf, 
    col.regions = "white", 
    alpha.regions = 0.1, 
    color = "grey50", 
    legend = FALSE,
    layer.name = "Study Area",
    map.type = "OpenStreetMap"
  ) +
  mapview(
    cell_summary, 
    zcol = "best_sf", 
    col.regions = sf_colors, 
    alpha.regions = 0.6,
    layer.name = "Best SF"
  ) +
  mapview(
    gateways, 
    label = "id",
    col.regions = "black", 
    cex = 5, 
    layer.name = "Gateways"
  )

# Display the map
map_out

```
